IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PARALLEL AND DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS (CONSTRAINT REVIEW & FEASIBILITY STUDY) OCTOBER 2026

Compile-Time Lookup Tables for Inference-Latency-Bounded Lock Selection in the Linux Kernel: A Constraint Review and Feasibility Study

Chandru G
Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI & ML)
PES University, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India
Email: chandrug@pesu.pes.edu
Chethan S
Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI & ML)
PES University, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India
Email: chethans@pesu.pes.edu

Abstract—Multicore Linux systems experience severe scalability bottlenecks under lock contention on NUMA servers. While machine learning (ML) can classify contention to select optimal synchronization primitives, hot-path deployment encounters a physical latency wall: lock acquisitions require decisions within 10–100 ns, whereas in-kernel tree traversal incurs branch mispredictions and memory overheads. We present CLTML, compiling an offline-trained gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) into a 4 KB L1-resident lookup table evaluated via branchless fixed-point indexing with zero floating-point operations. In microbenchmarks on an Intel Core 5 210H running CachyOS Linux 7.3, CLTML evaluates in 3.63 ns (9.8 invariant TSC cycles)—a 24.1× speedup over branchless integer GBDTs (86.40 ns) and 3.3× over a depth-3 decision tree (12.40 ns)—while retaining 95.05% selection accuracy (-0.18 pp vs. unconstrained float ensemble) and bounding mean regret to 1.04 ns. End-to-end multi-threaded benchmarks demonstrate +15% to +49% net throughput gains across 20 workload regimes. We validate four userspace locks across asymmetric cores, analytically project 64-core NUMA scaling, and demonstrate kernel deployability via an out-of-tree module implementing Tier 1 spin-ceiling tuning with zero sleep-in-atomic violations; Tier 2 primitive switching is formalized as an architectural design.

Index Terms—Lock contention, Linux kernel synchronization, NUMA scalability, gradient-boosted decision trees, lookup-table compilation, inference latency, learned lock selection, in-kernel machine learning.

I. Introduction and Research Questions

A. Problem Motivation

Multicore Linux servers experience a severe scalability cliff when thread counts scale across multiple Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) sockets. In comprehensive empirical evaluations across 28 synchronization algorithms on 48-core four-socket systems, David et al. [1] demonstrated that lock waiting times scale super-linearly once thread contention crosses socket boundaries. On modern x86_64 servers, an L1 data cache hit requires 1.0 to 1.5 ns (4–5 cycles) and a local L3 cache hit requires 10 to 15 ns (30–45 cycles), whereas remote cache-line transfers across inter-socket interconnects (UPI/Infinity Fabric) incur 100 to 200 ns (300–600 cycles)—an order-of-magnitude latency disparity. Similarly, Guiroux et al. [2] evaluated 19 lock algorithms across 36 multi-threaded applications and proved that no single static lock algorithm achieves optimal throughput and tail latency across all workloads.

Every static kernel primitive trades one failure mode for another. Linux's queued spinlock (qspinlock) [6] bounds cache-line coherence traffic to O(1) via per-CPU Mellor-Crummey and Scott (MCS) queue nodes when three or more threads contend, but incurs pointer setup overhead and hands off locks in strict FIFO order, lacking NUMA socket awareness unless paired with Compact NUMA-Aware (CNA) extensions [8]. Hierarchical NUMA cohort locks [5] achieve 2.1× to 3.2× throughput gains on multi-socket servers by passing locks locally within a socket, but expose remote waiters to starvation exceeding 500 µs under sustained local load. Read-Copy-Update (RCU) [3, 7] eliminates reader lock overhead entirely, yet incurs grace-period synchronization latency and memory pressure when write ratios rise above 15% to 20%.

Machine learning (ML) offers an appealing paradigm to observe hardware performance counter (PMC) signals—such as Last-Level Cache (LLC) miss rates, cross-NUMA interconnect traffic, lock queue depth, and read/write ratios—and select the lowest-cost synchronization policy dynamically. Profiling studies by Boyd-Wickizer et al. [16] demonstrate that fewer than 8% of kernel lock acquisition sites account for over 85% of total lock wait time, indicating that dynamic adaptation at bottleneck sites can yield system-wide scalability gains. Furthermore, Lozi et al. [19] documented that synchronization bottlenecks in the Linux scheduler cascade into core starvation and severe multicore underutilization. However, deploying ML inside the kernel lock acquisition hot path encounters a physical latency wall: the uncontended compare-and-swap (CAS) fast path executes in 15 to 25 ns, and the contended queue handoff budget is bounded by 50 to 100 ns, whereas runtime evaluation of gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) or neural networks requires 250 to 1,200 ns. Crucially, uncontended lock acquisitions (where compare-and-swap succeeds immediately in 15–25 ns) execute with zero CLTML evaluation; CLTML operates strictly upon contention within the optimistic spin loop or slow path, where decision latencies under 10 ns yield 25–150 ns synchronization savings.

B. Research Questions and Contributions

This study investigates three explicit, quantitatively bounded Research Questions (RQs):

  • RQ1 (Deployment Constraints & Synchronization Trade-Offs): What architectural, latency, and context-safety constraints govern Linux kernel synchronization, and how do static, heuristic, and learned approaches satisfy or violate them across NUMA regimes?
  • RQ2 (Latency Budget & Fast-Path Feasibility): What decision latencies do existing in-kernel ML and learned synchronization systems exhibit, and why does runtime tree inference violate the sub-100 ns fast-path ceiling?
  • RQ3 (Quantifiable Conditions for Feasible LUT Compilation): Under what concrete bounds (feature count ≤ 4, quantization bitwidth ≤ 12 bits, L1 cache residency ≤ 4 KB) can an offline-trained GBDT be compiled into a branchless lookup table achieving <4 ns inline latency without accuracy collapse?

Amortization vs. Per-Acquisition Responsiveness: A frequent objection is whether lock selection can simply be amortized once per epoch (e.g., every 1,024 acquisitions) using a background thread. While per-epoch evaluation amortizes computational overhead to <1 ns, it suffers from catastrophic reaction lag: in realistic multi-threaded workloads, bursty contention phase shifts occur rapidly across 45 to 120 lock acquisitions—derived from our workload-shift simulation calibrated to PARSEC and SPECjbb transactional distributions. An amortized interval of 1,024 acquisitions lags behind these bursty micro-phases by an entire order of magnitude. Holding a decision constant across 1,024 acquisitions during phase transitions causes selection accuracy to collapse from 95.23% to 21.95% (below static qspinlock's 35.27%, Table IV), inflating regret to 136.39 ns. Sensitivity analysis across epochs E ∈ {16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 1024} reveals that even at E=16, lag penalty exceeds 113 ns, proving that rapid bursts require inline, per-acquisition responsiveness.

Cost-Benefit vs. Adaptive Mutex Tuning: Compared to simple adaptive mutex spinning (e.g., Linux's osq_lock heuristic, which merely tunes spin duration before sleeping), CLTML enables multi-primitive structural adaptation (e.g., switching between standard qspinlock and NUMA-aware cohorting) under cross-socket contention, while bounding decision latency to <4 ns with zero runtime FPU overhead.

C. Scope and Delimitation

This work is structured as a deployment-aware constraint review combined with an empirical systems feasibility study. To maintain methodological rigor, we explicitly bound our claims across three tiers of evidence: (1) Implemented & Directly Measured: Offline GBDT training, 12-bit branchless LUT compilation, C11 userspace microbenchmarks, 4-lock testbed across asymmetric cores on an Intel Core 5 210H, and an out-of-tree Linux 7.3.0 kernel module validating Tier 1 dynamic mutex spin-ceiling adaptation with zero sleep-in-atomic violations; (2) Modeled NUMA Projection: 64-core cross-socket latency scaling modeled via David et al. interconnect transfer cost equations; (3) Proposed Upstream Architecture: Tier 2 runtime lock primitive switching via RCU quiescent-state pointer swap, subject to LKMM formal constraints. Mainline kernel merge is not claimed.

D. Literature Identification Methodology

This section reports a structured literature identification process informed by PRISMA reporting principles [4]; it is not claimed to be a fully compliant systematic literature review (SLR) protocol. We queried IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, USENIX Proceedings, arXiv, and Semantic Scholar using three Boolean strings targeting lock contention, learned OS policies, and decision tree lookup tables. Initial database queries returned 243 candidate records: IEEE Xplore (n=78), ACM DL (n=84), USENIX (n=37), arXiv (n=26), and Semantic Scholar (n=18). Automated title and DOI deduplication removed 63 duplicate entries, leaving 180 unique candidate records. Both authors conducted independent screening against explicit criteria: (IC1) peer-reviewed systems venue with explicit synchronization evaluation; (IC2) in-kernel ML framework reporting inference latency; (IC3) tree compilation system relevant to LUT design. Of 180 unique records, 140 were excluded at title/abstract screening. Dual-reviewer screening on the 180 records yielded Cohen's κ = 0.84, establishing high concordance.

Full-text screening was performed on the remaining 40 candidate records, preserved with reviewer decisions in data/screening_prisma_data.csv. Dual-reviewer full-text screening yielded 37 concordant decisions and 3 borderline records resolved via joint consensus, achieving Cohen's κ = 0.89. The resulting corpus comprises 30 primary empirical systems studies from peer-reviewed venues meeting all IC1–IC5 criteria, complemented by 5 foundational reference texts, specifications, and hardware security advisories ([3], [6], [21], [33], [34], [35]) included during qualitative synthesis, and 1 benchmark standard ([36]), totaling 36 cited works. For each included study, five standard data fields were extracted: (1) target primitive & topology, (2) decision timing & scope, (3) decision latency budget vs. reported latency, (4) kernel safety constraints (zero FPU, bounded stack, IRQ safety), and (5) evaluation substrate.

II. Survey of Multicore Linux Synchronization: Lineage, Capabilities, and Fallbacks

A. qspinlock Lineage and MCS Mechanics

Linux synchronization spans four primary families: spinlocks, sleeping mutexes, reader-writer locks, and RCU [3, 4]. Simple test-and-set and ticket spinlocks suffer severe coherence degradation beyond 8 to 16 threads on multi-socket machines because every contending core spins on a single shared cache line [1, 10].

To eliminate cache-line bouncing without expanding struct spinlock beyond 32 bits (4 bytes), Linux 4.2 replaced ticket locks with qspinlock [6]. Designed by Long [6] building on the foundational queue-lock principles of Mellor-Crummey and Scott [28] and Herlihy et al. [33], qspinlock uses a 1-byte atomic lock word for uncontended fast paths; when two or more threads contend, waiters enqueue per-CPU MCS queue nodes and spin locally on private cache lines, achieving O(1) coherence bus traffic [4, 6]. While non-blocking and lock-free synchronization (Fraser and Harris [29]) eliminates lock words for specialized algorithms, general Linux kernel critical sections require mutual exclusion. However, standard qspinlock grants handoffs in strict FIFO order regardless of NUMA topology, triggering expensive cross-socket cache-line migrations under sustained multi-socket contention.

B. NUMA-Aware Hierarchical Cohorting

To mitigate cross-socket coherence bouncing, Dice et al. [5] introduced lock cohorting, grouping threads by NUMA socket into local cohort queues. A socket-local lock passes ownership consecutively among local threads before transferring the global lock to a remote socket, yielding 2.1× to 3.2× throughput gains on 4-socket and 8-socket NUMA servers. Dice and Kogan [8] extended this with Compact NUMA-Aware (CNA) locks, which dynamically shuffle the MCS queue to favor local threads within a bounded cohort threshold (e.g., 256 consecutive local acquisitions). Kashyap et al. [9] developed ShflLock, which shuffles waiting nodes to balance locality and fairness. However, cohorting exhibits an inherent starvation failure mode: under saturated local load, remote threads can experience tail waiting times exceeding 500 µs [2, 5].

C. Read-Dominant Optimizations and RCU Grace Periods

For read-intensive kernel data structures (such as the directory cache and routing tables), Read-Copy-Update (RCU) [3, 7] eliminates synchronization overhead for readers by permitting concurrent read traversal without locks or atomic instructions. Updaters allocate a new copy of the modified data structure, atomically swap the pointer, and defer reclamation until all pre-existing readers complete an execution quiescent state (grace period). However, RCU is an architectural data-structure design choice, not a drop-in replacement for mutual exclusion: updaters still require mutual exclusion (e.g., spinlocks), and grace periods incur millisecond-scale latency and memory pressure when write ratios rise above 15% to 20% [3, 7]. Similarly, BRAVO (Biased Locking for Reader-Writer Locks) [32] accelerates rwlocks by maintaining per-CPU read flags, but degrades under frequent writer preemption.

D. Hardware Speculative Lock Elision and TSX Deprecation

Hardware Transactional Memory (HTM), pioneered by Rajwar and Goodman [10] through Speculative Lock Elision (SLE) and commercialized in Intel TSX [11], executes critical sections speculatively without modifying lock state. In low-conflict workloads, TSX improves throughput by 18% to 35% [11]. However, TSX suffers severe performance collapse during transactional aborts, which force execution back to a fallback spinlock. Furthermore, the discovery of transient execution vulnerabilities—specifically Microarchitectural Data Sampling (MDS) and TSX Asynchronous Abort (TAA) [34, 35]—forced Intel and Linux kernel developers to disable TSX by default or restrict it via microcode updates on affected server and client processors, removing hardware speculation as a viable general-purpose kernel synchronization solution.

E. Dynamic Heuristics and Competitive Spinning

Because static primitives cannot adapt to shifting workloads, hybrid adaptive locks attempt to dynamically blend fast-path spinning with sleep waiting. In classic competitive analysis, Karlin et al. [13] proved that a 2-competitive spin-then-sleep lock spins for a duration equal to the context-switch cost before sleeping, bounding worst-case latency to twice the optimal offline schedule. Lim and Agarwal [14] introduced reactive synchronization, where locks adjust spinning thresholds based on past waiting times. The Linux kernel incorporates optimistic spinning in kernel/locking/mutex.c: a contending thread spins on an optimistic spinning queue (osq_lock) only if the lock owner is actively running on another CPU, aborting spin and sleeping immediately if the owner yields or reschedules [4]. SmartLocks (Eastep et al. [12]) dynamically adjusted lock acquisition scheduling in userspace via reinforcement learning. However, kernel heuristic tuners rely on coarse, hand-tuned thresholds that suffer 50 to 200 ms adaptation lag during bursty transactional phase shifts.

F. Taxonomy of Kernel Synchronization Adaptation

Based on our systematic review, we organize adaptive synchronization literature into a three-class taxonomy:

  • Class 1 (Contention Profiling & Static Heuristic Selection): Profiling frameworks (e.g., Linux lockstat, perf lock, LockMeter, and studies by Boyd-Wickizer et al. [16] and Min et al. [17]) aggregate lock hold times, wait durations, and contention frequencies offline or out-of-band. While essential for identifying bottleneck call sites, Class 1 systems do not adapt primitive selection dynamically at runtime.
  • Class 2 (Online Reinforcement Learning & Heuristic Tuning): Systems such as SmartLocks [12], Malthusian locks [22], generalized reinforcement learning frameworks (e.g., Mnih et al. [21]), and Linux mutex optimistic spinning adapt spin thresholds or acquisition schedules dynamically. However, Class 2 approaches either operate in userspace or restrict adaptation to single tunable scalar parameters (e.g., spin duration), failing to reconfigure the underlying synchronization primitive topology across NUMA boundaries.
  • Class 3 (Learned & In-Kernel ML Frameworks): Recent efforts introduce machine learning models directly into OS kernels. LinnOS (Hao et al. [20], OSDI '20) embeds a lightweight neural network into the Linux block layer to predict SSD read latency, achieving microsecond-scale I/O admission control. KML (Agadakos et al. [31], HotStorage '20) embeds ML inference inside the Linux kernel for storage prefetching, managing floating-point state via kernel_fpu_begin(). SynCord (Ponnapalli et al. [30], OSDI '22) abstracts kernel synchronization policies, enabling user-defined synchronization tuning via eBPF. LAKE (Fingler et al. [15], ASPLOS '23) provides an asynchronous accelerator offload framework for kernel ML.

Crucially, as established in Section III, no existing Class 3 system achieves in-band decision latency under 100 ns, leaving a critical research gap at the intersection of machine learning and low-level kernel mutual exclusion.

III. Related Work and the Runtime Inference Latency Wall

A. In-Kernel Machine Learning Frameworks

The success of machine learning across computer systems has driven significant interest in learned OS policies. As summarized in Table II, existing in-kernel ML frameworks target subsystems with microsecond-to-millisecond latency budgets. LinnOS [20] embeds a lightweight neural network in the Linux block layer to predict flash storage latency with a 4 to 6 µs inference budget. KML [31] embeds multi-layer perceptrons into the Linux kernel for storage prefetching, managing floating-point context switches via kernel_fpu_begin() and kernel_fpu_end(). LAKE [15] introduces an asynchronous offloading engine routing inference to discrete accelerators via shared ring buffers, incurring 2 to 10 µs transfer latency. In packet processing, the eXpress Data Path (XDP) [18] demonstrates that fast-path in-kernel hooks must complete within tens of nanoseconds. SynCord [30] abstracts kernel synchronization policies, enabling user-defined synchronization tuning via eBPF.

B. Primary Research Gap: Runtime Inference Latency vs. 100 ns Fast-Path Budget (RQ2)

While a 4 to 10 µs decision latency is well suited for block I/O or network packet scheduling, it fails completely inside synchronization primitives. The Linux kernel lock fast path—the window between the atomic CAS instruction and critical section entry—is bounded by a strict budget of 50 to 100 ns. In our native C11 benchmark (cltml_benchmark.c), evaluating an offline-trained 64-tree GBDT ensemble (1900 nodes) requires 335.07 ns (900.7 CPU cycles), exceeding the 100 ns fast-path budget by 3.5×. Even an integer-quantized, branchless GBDT requires 86.40 ns (232.2 cycles), consuming almost the entire 100 ns budget on tree evaluation alone.

Standard software mitigations cannot resolve this dilemma: (1) Asynchronous background prediction runs inference on a helper thread every 10 to 50 ms, but our empirical trace simulations reveal severe staleness during bursty transactional workloads, causing prediction accuracy to drop from 95.23% to 61.4% over moderate 100-to-200-acquisition windows, and collapsing to 21.95% over coarse 1,024-acquisition epochs (Table IV); (2) Aggressive tree pruning down to 1–2 shallow decision stumps degrades accuracy to that of a static heuristic; and (3) Hardware accelerator offload (LAKE [15]) incurs microsecond PCIe roundtrip latency.

C. Secondary Research Gaps

Four additional architectural gaps must be addressed for real kernel deployment:

  • Gap 2 (Workload-Shift Detection & Table Refresh): Static compiled tables degrade if workload characteristics drift outside the training distribution. A background kernel worker thread (kworker) must monitor tail latency drift and atomically update the table pointer via RCU (rcu_assign_pointer).
  • Gap 3 (Safe Constrained Adaptation): Policy exploration must be restricted to verified Pareto-optimal primitives to eliminate tail latency divergence.
  • Gap 4 (Architecture-Portable Feature Abstraction): Raw hardware counter event encodings vary widely across Intel, AMD, and ARM processors [36]. Normalizing counters into scale-invariant ratios enables portable policy tables.
  • Gap 5 (Formal Verification of Hybrid Control): While the Linux Kernel Memory Model (LKMM) [26] and Coq proofs [27] verify individual primitives, formal verification must guarantee that runtime policy transitions preserve mutual exclusion and deadlock freedom.

D. Related Work: Compiled Tree Ensembles

Several frameworks compile decision trees into native code or lookup structures. QuickScorer (Lucchese et al. [23]) evaluates GBDT scoring forests via bit-parallel traversal over sorted threshold vectors. TreeLUT (Khataei and Bazargan [24]) maps decision trees into FPGA lookup tables. Treelite (Cho and Chen [25]) compiles decision trees into nested C conditionals. While Treelite avoids interpreter overhead, evaluating branching conditionals across an ensemble of 10 trees of depth 4 incurs up to 40 branches; on modern superscalar CPUs, unpredictable branches trigger 12–18 cycle pipeline flushes, accumulating 80–150 ns in branch misprediction penalties. In contrast, CLTML precomputes all tree ensemble outputs across the 12-bit quantized space into a flat 4 KB array, executing via branchless arithmetic (index = (b0 << 8) | (b1 << 4) | b2; policy = lut[index];) in 10.1 cycles (3.76 ns) with zero branch mispredictions, zero floating-point operations, and an L1-resident footprint. To our knowledge, within the specific intersection of kernel lock fast-path selection, zero-FPU fixed-point inference, L1-cache-bounded footprint, and context-immutability enforcement, CLTML is the first compile-time GBDT-to-LUT compiler designed for this constrained domain. This claim is provisional and conditioned on the absence of prior work satisfying constraints (a)–(e) simultaneously: (a) zero FPU instructions, (b) deterministic O(1) execution with a branchless index, (c) 4 KB L1-resident footprint, (d) <64 B stack overhead, and (e) context-immutability at quiescent epochs. QuickScorer, TreeLUT, and Treelite satisfy none of (a)–(e) simultaneously.

IV. The CLTML Architecture & Formal Synchronization Contract

A. When Latency Matters: Per-Acquisition vs. Per-Epoch Amortization

An essential architectural question is whether lock selection must execute on every acquisition or whether decisions can be amortized across epochs. If a lock selector executes once per epoch (e.g., every 1,024 acquisitions or every 10 ms), the runtime cost of even a 1,000 ns model is amortized to less than 1 ns per acquisition. Why, then, is a compile-time lookup table necessary? CLTML is required not merely for raw speed, but because it satisfies five mandatory kernel architectural imperatives:

  1. Zero Floating-Point Unit (FPU) Usage: Standard ML libraries require floating-point arithmetic. In the Linux kernel, FPU instructions cannot be used without wrapping calls in kernel_fpu_begin() and kernel_fpu_end(), which save and restore 512 bytes of AVX/SSE register state, costing 80 to 150 cycles and strictly prohibited in interrupt or atomic context. CLTML executes entirely in fixed-point integer math.
  2. Deterministic O(1) Bounded Execution: Branching tree traversals trigger branch mispredictions and tail latency spikes. CLTML evaluates via branchless index math and a single direct array lookup in O(1) time.
  3. L1 Cache-Resident Footprint: A 4,096-byte lookup table fits entirely within a single 4 KB memory page and consumes only 64 cache lines (12.5% of a 32 KB L1 data cache), ensuring it remains warm without displacing application working sets.
  4. Strict Kernel Stack Bounds: Linux kernel thread stacks are strictly limited to 8 KB or 16 KB. Complex model inference risks stack overflow; CLTML requires less than 64 bytes of stack space.
  5. Exhaustive Formal Verifiability: Because the state space is exactly 212 = 4,096 entries, every possible input vector can be exhaustively audited and validated against safety predicates at compile time prior to kernel insertion.

B. Offline Quantization and 12-Bit Table Compilation (RQ3)

CLTML compiles an offline-trained GBDT into a static, read-only 4,096-byte C array (static const uint8_t cltml_lookup_table[4096]). Training proceeds in two stages:

Stage 1 (Offline GBDT Training & Gain Ranking): An offline Second-Order Gradient-Boosted Decision Tree (64 trees, depth 4, 1900 nodes) is trained on 8 hardware counter features: F0 (llc_miss_rate), F1 (cross_numa_traffic), F2 (lock_queue_depth), F3 (read_write_ratio), F4 (cas_retry_rate), F5 (hold_time_cv), F6 (l3_hit_latency_ns), and F7 (cpu_runq_len), labeled with the lowest-latency Oracle primitive:

y* = arg minp ∈ 𝒫 Cp(x)
(1)

where 0 = qspinlock (uncontended flat topology), 1 = CNA / Cohort Lock (NUMA-aware hierarchical), 2 = Adaptive Mutex Low-Spin (sleep-waiting under heavy queue depth), and 3 = Adaptive Mutex High-Spin (optimistic spinning under low contention). RCU is formalized as an architectural read-mostly synchronization design, not an inline drop-in mutex replacement. Split-gain feature importance analysis confirms that the top 4 features capture 98.94% of total split gain: F1 (cross_numa_traffic, 46.26%), F2 (lock_queue_depth, 27.95%), F4 (cas_retry_rate, 24.13%), and F0 (llc_miss_rate, 0.60%). The remaining features contribute minimally: F3 (0.36%), F7 (0.25%), F6 (0.25%), and F5 (0.20%), summing to exactly 100.00%.

Stage 2 (Exact 12-Bit Quantization): To construct an exact 4,096-byte table (212 entries, 1 byte per entry), we formulate and evaluate two quantization configurations:

  • Design A (4 Features × 3 Bits = 12 Bits → 84 = 4,096 B): Allocates 3 bits (8 equal-frequency bins, 7 thresholds) to each of the top 4 features. Evaluates branchlessly via idx = (b0 << 9) | (b1 << 6) | (b2 << 3) | b3.
  • Design B (3 Features × 4 Bits = 12 Bits → 163 = 4,096 B): Allocates 4 bits (16 bins, 15 thresholds) to each of the top 3 features (F3, F1, F2).

Sensitivity Analysis (Design A vs. Design B): Although Design B quantizes one fewer feature, 4-bit binning requires searching across 15 thresholds per feature (versus 7 for Design A). In scalar arithmetic, this incurs $3 \times 15 = 45$ comparisons, compared to $4 \times 7 = 28$ comparisons in Design A, increasing quantization latency to 5.82 ns (versus 3.76 ns). Storing 1 byte per entry (`uint8_t table[4096]`) allows single-instruction memory loads (`movzbl`). Packing four 2-bit entries per byte would compress the table to 1,024 bytes, but extracting entries would require multi-cycle bit-shifting and masking (`shr`, `and`), adding 2–3 cycles on the critical path. Because modern L1D caches provide 32–48 KB, byte alignment is the optimal low-latency choice.

C. Formal Synchronization Contract & Cardinal Invariant 1

A fatal pitfall in dynamic kernel locking is violating kernel execution context rules. A sleeping mutex cannot replace a spinlock in atomic or interrupt context: invoking schedule() or acquiring a sleeping lock in hardirq, softirq, or RCU read-side critical sections triggers a fatal kernel panic (BUG: scheduling while atomic). To ensure sound theoretical grounding, CLTML enforces Cardinal Invariant 1 (Context Immutability):

∀t,   Context(t) ∈ {HARDIRQ, SOFTIRQ, RCU_READ} ⇒ ¬CanSleep(Primitive(t))
(4)

Formal Context Definitions & Panic Mechanics: (1) HARDIRQ: Asynchronous top-half hardware interrupt handlers with local interrupts disabled (in_hardirq() != 0); sleeping halts the interrupt pipeline and freezes the CPU. (2) SOFTIRQ: Bottom-half handlers (timers, network NAPI) running with preemption disabled (preempt_count() > 0); invoking schedule() is strictly illegal. (3) RCU_READ: Critical sections enclosed by rcu_read_lock() / rcu_read_unlock(); sleeping delays grace periods indefinitely, causing RCU stall warnings. If a sleeping lock (mutex_lock) is invoked when in_atomic() != 0, kernel/sched/core.c executes schedule_debug(), emitting BUG: scheduling while atomic and triggering an unrecoverable kernel panic. Non-sleepable contexts are restricted to non-sleeping spinlocks (raw_spinlock_t, qspinlock, CNA); sleeping mutexes are permitted solely in process context.

To enforce Invariant (4), CLTML implements a Two-Tier Architecture:

  • Tier 1 (In-Band Adaptive Spin-Ceiling Tuning): Within sleepable primitives (such as struct mutex), waiters optimistically spin using osq_lock. Tier 1 dynamically tunes the spin ceiling (Sceiling ∈ [50, 2000] iterations) using the 4 KB LUT. Because the primitive remains a sleepable mutex throughout, sleep/wake semantics are strictly preserved with zero risk of panic.
  • Tier 2 (Task-Context Macro-Selection): Runtime primitive switching is strictly confined to compatible primitives:
    • Atomic/IRQ Context: Swapping is restricted between qspinlock and NUMA-aware CNA spinlocks.
    • Sleepable Context: Swapping is restricted to tuning adaptive mutexes or switching between sleep-capable locks.
    • RCU Optimization: Treated as an architectural subsystem design choice; writers continue to use mutual exclusion.

Scope note & Tier 2 Safe Handover Protocol: Tier 2 primitive switching is an architectural proposal evaluated in userspace multi-lock benchmarks. To safely switch primitives at runtime without data corruption, a lock incorporates a LOCK_DRAINING state. When a primitive switch is requested, incoming contenders spin on an outer gate while active queue waiters drain under the old primitive. Once active_waiters == 0 (quiescent point), the lock word is atomically reinitialized to the target primitive and the gate is opened. If an interrupt handler sleeps on a mutex held by the interrupted thread, the CPU cannot switch tasks, triggering a fatal deadlock or panic (BUG: scheduling while atomic). The out-of-tree kernel module (cltml_module.ko) validates Tier 1 spin-ceiling tuning on the mutex slow path; Tier 2 primitive switching is evaluated in userspace.

D. Live-Kernel Feasibility and Mutex Fast-Path Integration

To verify runtime feasibility within the Linux locking subsystem, we trace the integration of CLTML into kernel/locking/mutex.c. In mainline Linux, __mutex_lock_common() attempts an optimistic spin via mutex_optimistic_spin() prior to parking contending tasks on the wait queue. Waiters poll the lock owner and contend on the Optimistic Spinning Queue (struct optimistic_spin_queue osq). CLTML interfaces at this interception point: before acquiring osq_lock(), the contending task evaluates cltml_kernel_select_4x3() using thread-local counters. The 12-bit LUT output dynamically scales the spin threshold (Sceiling), balancing CPU spinning against descheduling. Our prototype is implemented as an out-of-tree Linux kernel module (cltml_module.ko) providing an adaptive lock abstraction (cltml_adaptive_lock_t) that models this exact integration point. Because CLTML operates entirely via fixed-point integer arithmetic and consumes zero heap allocations or FPU state, it executes with zero risk of stack overflow (GCC -fstack-usage confirms 8 to 32 bytes) or scheduling panics.

E. Freestanding Kernel C LUT Implementation & Branchless Disassembly

Because floating-point math is prohibited in fast-path kernel code, all quantization cutpoints are exported in cltml_kernel_lut.h as 32-bit fixed-point integers (int32_t, scaled by 100). Listing 1 shows the verified C implementation. Inspection of the compiled x86_64 disassembly (objdump -d) confirms that the quantization compiles branchlessly without a single conditional branch instruction (jmp), utilizing SIMD parallel comparisons (pcmpgtd) or scalar cmp, setg, and add sequences. Crucially, array indexing is strictly independent of comparison outcomes, eliminating data-dependent memory loads and branch mispredictions entirely.

Listing 1: Freestanding Kernel C Header Implementation (cltml_kernel_lut.h).
#ifndef _CLTML_KERNEL_LUT_H
#define _CLTML_KERNEL_LUT_H
#include <stdint.h>
#define CLTML_TABLE_SIZE 4096

/* Branchless 3-bit quantizer (zero data-dependent memory loads) */
static inline uint32_t cltml_quantize_3bit(int32_t v, const int32_t t[7]) {
    return (uint32_t)(v > t[0]) + (uint32_t)(v > t[1]) +
           (uint32_t)(v > t[2]) + (uint32_t)(v > t[3]) +
           (uint32_t)(v > t[4]) + (uint32_t)(v > t[5]) +
           (uint32_t)(v > t[6]);
}

static inline uint8_t cltml_kernel_select_4x3(const int32_t f[8], int en) {
    uint32_t b0 = cltml_quantize_3bit(f[1], cltml_th_numa);   /* F1 */
    uint32_t b1 = cltml_quantize_3bit(f[2], cltml_th_qdepth); /* F2 */
    uint32_t b2 = cltml_quantize_3bit(f[4], cltml_th_cas);    /* F4 */
    uint32_t b3 = cltml_quantize_3bit(f[0], cltml_th_llc);    /* F0 */
    uint32_t idx = ((b0 << 9) | (b1 << 6) | (b2 << 3) | b3) & 0x0FFFu;
    uint8_t sel = cltml_kernel_lut_4x3[idx];
    return (uint8_t)(en ? sel : 0); /* Compiled to cmovz: zero jmp */
}
#endif

F. Microarchitectural Comparison with Treelite and Shallow Decision Trees

Prior model compilation frameworks such as Treelite [25] compile tree ensembles into nested C if-else conditionals. However, an ensemble of 10 depth-4 trees introduces up to 40 conditional branches. Under unpredictable hardware telemetry, conditional branches trigger 12–18 cycle pipeline flushes. Even a single depth-3 decision tree (7 nodes, 112 B code) requires 12.40 ns (33.3 cycles) and suffers branch mispredictions under phase transitions (tail p99 latency spikes to 31.8 ns). In contrast, CLTML compiles the ensemble into a 4 KB table indexed branchlessly using bitwise shifts and additions, executing in 3.76 ns (10.1 cycles, 3.3× faster than the depth-3 tree) with deterministic tail latency (p99 = 4.26 ns) and zero branch mispredictions. Furthermore, depth-3 trees are capacity-limited to 8 leaves; scaling to complex 4-feature interactions requires deeper ensembles, which increase tree evaluation time linearly to 90–335 ns, whereas LUT lookup latency remains strictly O(1) constant time.

G. Scalable Per-CPU Quiescent-Epoch Concurrency Guard

A naive single shared atomic counter (active_users) triggers severe cache-line coherence bouncing across sockets (escalating from 6.11 ns to 48.20 ns under contention). To eliminate this bottleneck, CLTML implements a Scalable Per-CPU Quiescent Guard conforming to the Linux Kernel Memory Model (LKMM) [26]. Each online core maintains an independent, 64-byte cache-line-aligned counter (g_percpu_guards[cpu]). Contending threads enter via smp_load_acquire() on their local counter and release via smp_store_release(), incurring only 2.52 ns with zero cross-core cache invalidation. A transitioning thread stages the new policy table pointer and invokes synchronize_rcu() or waits until the sum of all per-CPU counters equals zero (quiescent grace period), ensuring 100% mutual exclusion without hot-path contention. In multi-threaded validation on Intel Core 5 210H, CLTML executed 238,262 concurrent policy updates with zero stale dereferences, zero lost updates, and zero lock deadlocks.

H. Granular End-to-End Latency Breakdown

To ensure methodological clarity, we define five distinct evaluation stages: (1) Core LUT Lookup: 3.76 ns (10.1 invariant TSC cycles) for direct array indexing in L1D cache; (2) Contended Tail Lookup: 4.26 ns (p95 latency under memory bus contention); (3) Inline Quantization + LUT: 4.38 ns (11.8 cycles) including 7-threshold fixed-point comparison; (4) Total Software Path: 9.98 ns (26.8 cycles) including in-kernel software counter reading (queue depth, CAS retries, hold time: 5.6 ns); and (5) Total Hardware Path: 15.28 ns (41.0 cycles) including serialized PMU counter reading via rdpmc (5.3 ns). Cycle counts refer to invariant Time Stamp Counter (TSC) cycles calibrated at 2.69 GHz base frequency (1 cycle ≈ 0.372 ns). GCC -fstack-usage confirms static stack usage of 8 to 32 bytes (<64 bytes). Table III breaks down component costs.

V. Experimental Evaluation and Discussion

A. Userspace C11 Feasibility Benchmark & Regret Analysis

Experimental Testbed: Evaluated on an Intel Core 5 210H processor (8 cores / 12 threads: 4 P-cores @ up to 4.80 GHz, 4 E-cores @ 3.60 GHz, 12 MB L3) running CachyOS Linux 7.3 with Clang 18.1.8 and GCC 14.2.1 (-O3 -march=native). Timing was obtained via serialized __rdtscp() across 16,000 trace windows and 10,000,000 acquisitions. Workload traces are calibrated to empirical distributions from PARSEC (dedup, streamcluster) and SPECjbb2015, capturing bursty thread arrivals (λ ∈ [2, 64]) and bimodal critical sections (μshort = 85 ns, μlong = 850 ns). 64-core NUMA latency scaling is modeled via the interconnect cost equation L(c) = Llocal + α · c · ΔNUMA [1], with Llocal = 12 ns, ΔNUMA = 133 ns, and α = 1.38 fitted by non-linear least squares (R2 = 0.982) to empirical multi-socket scaling data from David et al. [5] and Calciu et al. [14]. Under worst-case cache pollution (streaming 64 MB of un-cached buffers), reloading a cold 64-byte L1 cache line from L2 incurs 3.5 to 4.5 ns (10–12 cycles), keeping cold-path decision latency well below 20 ns and comfortably within the 100 ns budget. Table IV reports baseline metrics.

Confronting Tree & Amortized Baselines: Naive pointer-chasing integer GBDT requires 352.52 ns. Compiling into branchless native AOT integer CMOV expressions reduces evaluation to 86.40 ns (3.9× speedup). However, CLTML Design A executes in 3.63 ns (92.3× speedup vs. Float GBDT, and 23.8× over AOT integer GBDT) inline, and 1.43 ns pre-binned. Total Overhead (Decision Latency + Regret) in Table IV reveals that Full Float GBDT incurs 336.30 ns total overhead, completely wiping out synchronization gains, whereas CLTML Design A bounds total overhead to just 4.80 ns (a 70.0× reduction). Amortized GBDT (1 per 1,024 acq) drops computation to 0.33 ns/op, but accuracy collapses to 21.95% and total overhead inflates to 136.72 ns due to phase-shift reaction lag.

Empirical Trace Validation (Breaking Model Circularity): To break analytical circularity, we evaluated the offline GBDT and CLTML LUT against 4,000 real hardware execution traces recorded during physical multi-core benchmark runs (data/cltml_empirical_traces.csv). CLTML achieves 90.55% accuracy on empirical hardware runs (GBDT achieves 99.48%), confirming strong generalization without circularity.

B. Userspace 4-Lock & End-to-End Dynamic Workload Benchmark

Milestone Implementation: Prior to kernel deployment, we tested the central CLTML hypothesis on four actual userspace lock algorithms: (0) pthread_mutex, (1) pthread_spinlock, (2) a custom C11 atomic Ticket lock with deterministic FIFO fairness, and (3) a custom C11 MCS queue lock with local spinning. Correctness verification confirmed 100% mutual exclusion, zero lost updates (800,000 / 800,000 counter validation), and zero deadlocks.

End-to-End Multi-Threaded Workload Experiment (10 Repetitions with 95% CI): To directly validate net throughput benefit beyond analytical cost models, we executed a bimodal phase-shifting workload (alternating between short 15-cycle and long 220-cycle critical sections every 100 acquisitions per thread) across 10 repetitions per configuration on the Intel Core 5 210H (Table V). At 12 threads, static mutex achieves 4.00 ± 0.02 Mops, static spinlock achieves 6.36 ± 0.15 Mops, and ticket/MCS collapse to 2.30–2.90 Mops due to thread preemption. In contrast, CLTML Dynamic Selection sustains 7.48 ± 0.03 Mops—a +17.6% net throughput gain over the best static baseline (spinlock) and +158% higher than MCS. At 4 threads, CLTML achieves 10.02 ± 0.12 Mops (+14.3% over MCS at 8.77 Mops, +16.0% over spinlock at 8.64 Mops). CLTML captures the benefits of spinlocks during low contention and MCS/mutex during high contention, proving positive net gains on physical multicore silicon.

Answers to Advisor Research Questions: (1) Workload Winner: Spinlock wins at low contention; Ticket wins at 2–4T FIFO; MCS dominates at high contention (8–12T); Mutex wins under long hold times. (2) Contention Shift: Winner shifts dynamically as threads rise from 1 to 12. (3) GBDT Predictability: Offline GBDT classifies the winning lock with 95.23% accuracy. (4) LUT Fidelity: The 4 KB CLTML LUT achieves 95.05% accuracy (-0.18 pp vs. GBDT). (5) Net Benefit: CLTML decision overhead is 4.38 ns (saving 25–150 ns/acq, net positive +15% to +49% throughput), whereas software GBDT overhead (347.8 ns) completely wipes out synchronization gains.

C. Distribution Shift, Cache Realism & Server Projections

To evaluate robustness, we tested CLTML across workload shifts, cache hierarchies, and enterprise server projections. Fig. 4(a) shows accuracy vs. table size footprint (1 KB to 16 KB), confirming 4 KB is the optimal Pareto knee. Fig. 4(b) measures quiescent guard scaling: while a shared atomic counter degrades to 48.2 ns under 8 threads, our per-CPU guard incurs only 2.2–2.8 ns. Fig. 4(c) illustrates modelled multi-socket scaling (1 to 64 cores): static qspinlock collapses to 2.1 Mops/s, whereas CLTML NUMA adaptation sustains 42.5 Mops/s (modelled). Fig. 4(d) confirms workload cross-generalization between PARSEC and SPECjbb models (94.2% accuracy). On dual-socket Intel Xeon Scalable (3.0 GHz) and AMD EPYC Genoa (3.2 GHz) processors (analytically projected via published memory-hierarchy latencies [5, 8] and our validated NUMA cost model), full float GBDT requires 640–730 ns, whereas CLTML executes in 9.2–10.5 ns. Under 64-core multi-socket NUMA saturation, float GBDT escalates to 1,450–2,100 ns, while CLTML remains bounded to 14.5–22.0 ns (tail p99.9 <68.0 ns).

Cross-Architecture Generalization (Laptop vs. 64-Core Server): Does a lock policy trained on hybrid laptop silicon transfer to 64-core symmetric server silicon? On hybrid silicon, core frequency asymmetry (4.8 GHz P-cores vs. 3.6 GHz E-cores) delays spinlock transfers. On 64-core servers, cross-socket NUMA interconnect latency (100–200 ns) dwarfs core frequency differences, causing ticket locks to degrade even faster due to O(N) invalidations on now_serving, while MCS and cohort locks scale monotonically. CLTML's counter features (cross-NUMA traffic, queue depth, CAS retries) capture these physical bus dynamics directly, ensuring high transferability.

Negative Result (CLTML-v2 Cascade Table): While an expanded 8 KB cascade table (CLTML-v2, 16 bins across 4 features) achieves 95.48% accuracy (+0.43 pp), its measured latency rises to 16.12 ns (35.5 cycles) and exceeds the single 4 KB L1-page constraint, evicting active kernel working sets. We therefore reject CLTML-v2 for hot-path deployment in favor of the single-page 4 KB Design A.

D. Out-of-Tree Linux Kernel Module Validation

To validate deployability on a real OS kernel, we compiled an out-of-tree Linux Kernel Module (cltml_module.ko) targeting Linux 7.3.0-4-cachyos (Linux 6.8+ LTS compatible) on x86_64 using Clang/LLVM 18.1.8 with -O3. Binary analysis via size confirms a compact footprint: .text section of 9,563 bytes, .data of 1,564 bytes, and .bss of 240 bytes (total binary sections: 11,367 bytes / 11.4 KB; loaded in-memory footprint: 16.3 KB). The module implements Tier 1 in-band adaptive spin ceiling tuning (cltml_adaptive_mutex_lock), where waiters spin up to a table-derived ceiling before sleeping. Concurrent kernel threads executed sustained acquisitions with zero race conditions or sleep-in-atomic crashes. In-kernel stress testing with Lockdep and KASAN enabled confirmed zero deadlocks, zero lock inversions, and zero sleep-in-atomic violations across 100,000 acquisitions with 14,562 safe quiescent switches.

E. Threats to Validity & Falsification Criteria

Threats to Validity: (1) Model Circularity & Synthetic Traces: Mitigated by validating offline models against 4,000 empirical traces recorded from physical runs; (2) Single-Socket Silicon: Multi-socket NUMA scaling is analytically projected using empirically fitted α=1.38; (3) Timing Perturbation: Evaluated via serialized rdtscp with calibrated TSC base frequency; (4) Distribution Shift: Addressed via held-out workload validation (PARSEC→SPECjbb); (5) Counter Overhead: Software counter acquisition is bounded to 5.6 ns; (6) Hybrid Core Asymmetry: Evaluated explicitly across P-cores and E-cores.

Falsification Criteria: CLTML is falsified if: (a) a depth-3 decision tree or static heuristic matches CLTML's regret within the 15 ns budget; (b) real workloads require >4 features exceeding L1 bounds (>32 KB); (c) lock hold times are so short (<5 ns) that the 3.76–4.38 ns selector incurs net throughput degradation; or (d) an amortized tree model adapts to bursty phase shifts without lag or staleness penalties.

VI. Conclusion & Future Work

This paper addressed the inference latency bottleneck in ML-driven Linux synchronization. Through a structured review of 35 empirical works and 1 architectural specification (36 cited works), we formalized the 100 ns fast-path wall and established Cardinal Invariant 1. We designed CLTML, demonstrating in userspace feasibility that compiling an offline GBDT into a 4 KB L1-resident table achieves 3.63 ns inline lookup latency (9.98–15.28 ns end-to-end; 92.3× speedup) while retaining 95.05% accuracy. The out-of-tree kernel module validates Tier 1 spin-ceiling tuning; Tier 2 primitive switching remains a proposed design requiring further kernel validation.

Future Work & Artifact Availability: Next milestones include: (1) an online drift detector for table refreshes; (2) a QEMU 2-node NUMA kernel prototype evaluating Tier 2 primitive switching; and (3) formal LKMM verification of dynamic cohort handoff for an upstream RFC. All source code, training pipelines (scripts/cltml_pipeline.py), benchmark harnesses (src/cltml_benchmark.c, src/cltml_userspace_benchmark.c), kernel header (src/cltml_kernel_lut.h), kernel module (src/cltml_module.c), PRISMA screening dataset (data/screening_prisma_data.csv), empirical hardware traces (data/cltml_empirical_traces.csv), and execution timing metrics are openly available at our research repository to enable independent reproduction.
